title: Board memo: Basel III proposal, GSIB surcharge proposal, and standardized approach proposal
summary: The Federal Reserve Board of Governors is being asked to approve three capital regulatory proposals for public comment: a Basel III framework revision for the largest internationally active banks (Category I and II), a GSIB surcharge calculation revision, and a standardized approach modification for smaller banks (Category III/IV and below). The proposals would collectively reduce aggregate common equity Tier 1 capital requirements for Category I and II firms by 4.8 percent, with the largest drivers being a -3.8 percent reduction from the GSIB surcharge revision and -4.3 percent from proposed stress testing changes (per staff estimates subject to revision through public comment process).
key_points: Basel III proposal targets Category I and II firms (largest, most internationally active banks), simplifying to a single set of risk-based capital calculations and better aligning requirements with risk including additional credit risk factors
GSIB surcharge proposal would revise the calculation methodology for the capital add-on applicable to globally systemically important banks, improving measurement of systemic risk
Standardized approach proposal would revise the U.S. standardized approach for Category III/IV firms and smaller banks, better aligning capital requirements with traditional lending activities
Proposed changes would remove capital deduction for certain mortgage servicing assets to increase bank incentive for mortgage origination and servicing
Category I and II firms: Basel III NPR (+1.4%), GSIB Surcharge NPR (-3.8%), AOCI Requirement (+3.1%), Stress Test Changes (-4.3%), Total (-4.8%)
Category III and IV firms: Total CET1 reduction of 5.2 percent; Smaller banking organizations: Total CET1 reduction of 7.8 percent
why_it_matters: This memo outlines significant potential changes to bank capital regulation that would affect how the largest U.S. banks calculate and hold capital. The net reduction in capital requirements (approximately 5-8% across bank categories per staff estimates) could free up capital for lending or other activities. Changes to GSIB surcharge methodology could alter competitive dynamics among the largest banks. Removal of mortgage servicing asset capital deductions could boost mortgage market activity. Note: These are proposed regulatory actions pending public comment and formal publication in the Federal Register.
macro_context: The proposals aim to reduce excessive requirements for traditional banking activities that may have accelerated migration of activities from regulated banks to non-banks. The Fed states this would enhance firms' ability to provide financial services while maintaining banking system safety and soundness. The document acknowledges that since the 2007-09 crisis, large banks have more than doubled their capital levels (an increase of more than $1 trillion), contributing to the robustness of the framework.
market_structure_context: These regulatory capital changes would affect the competitive landscape between banks and non-bank financial institutions, potentially reducing regulatory arbitrage incentives. The simplification of the Basel III framework for large banks and the standardized approach for smaller banks represents a structural shift in how capital requirements are applied across the banking sector. Note: This is an internal board memo, not the formal regulatory proposal - the actual proposals will be published in the Federal Register pending Board approval.
